hints: Look closely at what changes and what stays the same between citric acid and tricarballylic acid, especially the functional groups.
Notice the central carbon loses its $\text{OH}$ group in stage 1 to form an alkene Q, which is a classic dehydration of an alcohol.
Think about what reagent adds $\text{H}_2$ across a $\text{C=C}$ bond in stage 2 while leaving the three $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups untouched.
walkthrough:
**Compare the start and end structures**

Citric acid has a tertiary alcohol group, $\text{C-OH}$, in the middle plus three $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups. Tricarballylic acid has the same three $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups but the $\text{OH}$ is replaced by $\text{H}$, so the central $\text{C-OH}$ becomes $\text{CH}$.

Overall change:
$$\text{C-OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}$$

**Work out stage 1 to make Q**

A direct $\text{OH}$ to $\text{H}$ swap is not one step. The usual route is to first eliminate water to make a $\text{C=C}$ double bond. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong dehydrating agent that removes $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from an alcohol.

$$\text{R}_2\text{C(OH)-CH}_2\text{R} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C=CHR} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Work out stage 2 to finish the job**

Intermediate Q is therefore an unsaturated tricarboxylic acid containing $\text{C=C}$. Adding $\text{H}_2$ across the double bond with Ni catalyst gives the saturated product.

$$\text{C=C} + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} \text{CH-CH}$$

**Choose the reagent pair**

Stage 1 needs dehydration with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, and stage 2 needs electrophilic addition of hydrogen with $\text{H}_2(g)$ and Ni. This combination leaves the carboxylic acid groups unchanged.

options.A: Correct. Concentrated H2SO4 dehydrates the tertiary alcohol in citric acid to give the alkene Q, then H2 with Ni reduces the C=C bond to give tricarballylic acid. Neither reagent attacks the CO2H groups.
options.B: Stage 1 is correct but stage 2 is wrong. LiAlH4 is a powerful reducing agent that reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols, so it would destroy the three CO2H groups instead of just hydrogenating the C=C bond.
options.C: Both stages are wrong. LiAlH4 in stage 1 would reduce the CO2H groups to alcohols rather than dehydrate the OH group. Dilute H2SO4(aq) in stage 2 does not add H2 across a C=C bond.
options.D: Stage 2 is correct but stage 1 is wrong. NaOH(aq) would simply neutralise the carboxylic acids to form carboxylate salts, not eliminate water to form an alkene. Dehydration needs concentrated H2SO4, not aqueous alkali.
